learn: How images become tokens for a language model
Audio tokenization and shared multimodal token spaces
The growth of context length and what it costs
Frontier reasoning, tool use and computer use
Case studies: assembling the full LLM stack
Frontier risks and how capable systems are evaluated
intro.why: This final session connects the course to where the field is heading: models that see, hear, read very long inputs, reason at length and act, and the engineering and safety work that makes them usable.
prereq: All previous sessions, especially M5, M12–M15

sections.title: Images as tokens
sections.plain: Cut an image into small squares, turn each into a vector, and feed them to the model like words.
sections.body:
A Vision Transformer splits an H × W image into P × P patches, flattens each, and linearly embeds it into a vector: one token per patch. Worked: 224 × 224 with 16 × 16 patches → 14 × 14 = 196 tokens of 768 numbers each.

Vision–language models connect such an encoder to an LLM with a projector (a linear layer or small MLP) mapping vision features (e.g. 768-d) into the LLM's embedding space (e.g. 4096-d). Image tokens are then interleaved with text tokens: "[image] … [/image] What is in the picture?". Training aligns the spaces on image–caption data, then instruction-tunes on visual tasks.

Resolution drives cost: 896² → 3,136 tokens, so models tile large images, pool or compress patch tokens, or use dynamic resolution. Some models instead generate images by predicting discrete image tokens or by pairing with diffusion decoders.

sections.title: Audio and shared token spaces
sections.plain: Sound is also chopped into short pieces and turned into tokens, so one model can listen, read and talk.
sections.body:
Two audio routes:

  • Continuous encoder features: a speech encoder produces one vector per short frame (e.g. 20 ms → 50 per second; 10 s → 500 frames), projected into the LLM space for understanding tasks.
  • Discrete codec tokens: a neural audio codec compresses audio into codes from K residual codebooks at a frame rate (8 codebooks × 75 Hz → 6,000 tokens for 10 s). These can be predicted autoregressively to generate speech.

A shared token space lets one Transformer process text, image and audio tokens in a single sequence, enabling speech-to-speech assistants and cross-modal reasoning. Challenges: audio is token-hungry, latency matters for conversation, and modalities must be balanced in training.

sections.title: Long-context growth
sections.plain: Models can now read hundreds of thousands of words at once, but longer inputs cost much more.
sections.body:
Context windows have grown by orders of magnitude in a few years: from around 2k tokens to 32k–128k and to a million or more. Costs grow with length: KV memory linearly (1 GiB at 2k → 488 GiB at 1M for a 32-layer, 4096-wide model without GQA) and attention work quadratically (2k → 1M is ~488× longer but ~238,000× more token pairs).

Enablers come from across the course: FlashAttention and Ring Attention (M4), RoPE scaling and long-context training curricula (M3), GQA/MLA and paged, quantized caches (M5–M6), and sparse or hybrid attention. A long window is not the same as using it well: models can miss information in the middle, so long-context ability is measured with retrieval and reasoning tests across positions, and RAG remains complementary (M12).

sections.title: Frontier reasoning and tool use
sections.plain: The newest systems think at length, use tools and computers, and handle several kinds of input at once.
sections.body:
• Reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable rewards spend many tokens thinking before answering; performance scales with test-time compute (M11).
  • Native tool use: search, code execution and APIs inside the reasoning loop give grounded facts and exact computation.
  • Computer use: agents read screens and operate software through clicks and typing.
  • Multimodality: unified models read and produce text, images and speech.
  • Long-horizon agents work for hours on coding and research with memory and planning.

The limiting factors shift from raw capability to reliability (compounding errors), cost and latency, and oversight of autonomous actions.

sections.title: Case studies: the integrated stack
sections.plain: Real products combine nearly every technique from this course; each layer adds value but also cost and risk.
sections.body:
A typical enterprise assistant combines: a base model chosen by scaling and serving budget (M2–M3); fine-tuning and alignment for house style and safety (M7, M9); prompts and structured outputs (M10); retrieval over company documents (M12); an agent loop with tools such as search and SQL (M13); guardrails (M15); efficient serving with quantization, batching and caching (M5–M6); and an evaluation suite gating every release (M14).

Worked (ex2): 3 agent steps × 2,360 prompt tokens (800 system + 60 user + 5 × 300 retrieved) = 7,080 input and 750 output tokens → about $0.0325 per request at illustrative prices of $3/M input and $15/M output ($3,249 per 100,000 requests); prefix caching of the system prompt cuts it to about $0.026. Lessons from case studies: start simple, measure, add components only when evaluation shows they help, and design for failure.

sections.title: Frontier risks and evaluation
sections.plain: More capable models can do more good and more harm, so their risks are tested as carefully as their skills.
sections.body:
Capability growth brings new concerns: misuse of dangerous knowledge, autonomous agents acting at scale, persuasion and deception, privacy, concentration of power, and over-reliance on fluent but wrong outputs. Bigger is not automatically safer: safety must be engineered and measured at each capability level.

Practices: dangerous-capability evaluations before release, red teaming including agentic scenarios, staged deployment and access controls, monitoring and incident response, interpretability and scalable-oversight research, and transparency documents (system cards, usage policies). Evaluation of frontier systems combines capability benchmarks, safety tests, long-horizon agent tasks and expert human assessment, and must keep pace as benchmarks saturate.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Small models matter too: distilled, quantized models run on phones and laptops for privacy and latency.
  • Open vs closed models trade transparency and customisation against managed safety and convenience.
  • Data is the moat: evaluation sets and domain data often matter more than the choice of base model.
  • The fundamentals persist: tokens, attention, memory, decoding and evaluation underlie every new modality and agent.

code.title: Image patches, audio tokens and a shared space
code.explain: Splits a 224 × 224 image into 196 patches of 768 numbers, embeds and projects them from 768-d into a 4096-d language space, lists token counts at higher resolutions (441, 784, 3,136), converts 10 s of audio into 500 encoder frames or 6,000 codec tokens, and prints an interleaved image–text sequence.
mistakes: Forgetting that image tokens consume context.
Assuming audio is as cheap as its transcript.
code.code:
"""Turning images and audio into tokens, and projecting them into a language model's embedding space."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Images as patch tokens (Vision Transformer style)
H = W = 224; P = 16; C = 3
n_patches = (H // P) * (W // P)
print(f"image {H}x{W}x{C}, patch {P}x{P} -> {H//P} x {W//P} = {n_patches} patch tokens, each {P*P*C} numbers")
img = rng.random((H, W, C))
patches = img.reshape(H // P, P, W // P, P, C).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4).reshape(n_patches, P * P * C)
d_vision, d_llm = 768, 4096
W_patch = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (P * P * C, d_vision))
vis_tokens = patches @ W_patch
W_proj = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (d_vision, d_llm))             # the adapter/projector learned during multimodal training
llm_tokens = vis_tokens @ W_proj
print(f"patch embeddings {vis_tokens.shape} -> projected into the LLM space {llm_tokens.shape}")
for side in (336, 448, 896):
    print(f"  {side}x{side} image -> {(side // P) ** 2} tokens")

# Audio: frames or discrete codec tokens
sr, secs = 16000, 10
frame_ms = 20
frames = secs * 1000 // frame_ms
print(f"\n{secs} s of audio at {sr} Hz = {sr*secs:,} samples -> {frames} frames of {frame_ms} ms (encoder tokens)")
codebooks, rate = 8, 75
print(f"neural codec with {codebooks} residual codebooks at {rate} Hz -> {codebooks*rate*secs:,} discrete tokens for {secs} s")

# A shared token space: text and image tokens in one sequence
seq = ["[image]"] + [f"img{i}" for i in range(3)] + ["...", "[/image]", "What", "is", "in", "the", "picture", "?"]
print("\ninterleaved sequence:", " ".join(seq))
print(f"a {n_patches}-token image costs about as much context as {n_patches} words of text")

code.title: Context growth and an integrated-stack budget
code.explain: Tabulates KV-cache size and attention pairs at 2k, 32k and 1M tokens (1 → 16 → 488 GiB without GQA; 238,000× more attention pairs from 2k to 1M), then estimates tokens and cost for a 3-step RAG agent ($0.0325 per request; $0.026 with prefix caching).
mistakes: Ignoring that each agent step re-sends context.
Quoting window size as effective use.
code.code:
"""How context length growth changes cost, and an integrated-stack cost estimate for a RAG agent."""
eras = [("early large LMs", 2048), ("later chat models", 32768), ("long-context models", 1_000_000)]
L, d, b = 32, 4096, 2
for name, n in eras:
    kv = 2 * L * d * b * n / 2**30
    print(f"{name:22s}: {n:>9,} tokens; full KV cache {kv:8.1f} GiB (32 layers, width 4096, 16-bit, no GQA); attention pairs {n*n:.1e}")
print(f"growth 2k -> 1M is {1_000_000/2048:.0f}x in length but {(1_000_000/2048)**2:,.0f}x in pairwise attention work")
print("hence GQA/MLA, FlashAttention, ring attention, RoPE scaling and retrieval all matter together")

# Integrated stack: per-request token budget for a RAG agent
system, user, chunks, chunk_len, steps, out = 800, 60, 5, 300, 3, 250
prompt = system + user + chunks * chunk_len
total_in = prompt * steps                       # each agent step re-sends context (no caching)
total_out = out * steps
price_in, price_out = 3.0, 15.0                 # $ per million tokens (illustrative)
cost = total_in / 1e6 * price_in + total_out / 1e6 * price_out
print(f"\nper request: {steps} agent steps x {prompt} prompt tokens = {total_in:,} input, {total_out} output tokens")
print(f"illustrative cost ${cost:.4f} per request -> ${cost*100_000:,.0f} per 100,000 requests")
cached = (system * steps * 0.1 + (prompt - system) * steps) / 1e6 * price_in + total_out / 1e6 * price_out
print(f"with prefix caching of the system prompt (90% discount on cached tokens): ${cached:.4f} per request")
